item.title: Bound Entanglement with Negative Partial Transpose Exists
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a decades‑old question by demonstrating the first explicit example of a negative‑partial‑transpose (NPT) state that is nevertheless bound entangled, overturning the long‑standing belief that NPT automatically implies distillability. By proving that the Werner state on an 8 × 8 system cannot be distilled even with unlimited copies or separable operations, it shows that distillable entanglement is neither additive nor convex—fundamental properties assumed in many theoretical frameworks. The result forces a re‑examination of entanglement‑based benchmarks for quantum hardware, reminding developers that simple PPT tests are insufficient to guarantee usable entanglement. It also opens new avenues for exploring exotic resource states that could be harnessed—or must be avoided—in future quantum protocols.

We show that the Werner state $ρ= (23 I - 3\,\mathrm{SWAP})/1448$ on $\mathbb{C}^8 \otimes \mathbb{C}^8$ has a negative partial transpose and is bound entangled: no LOCC protocol can distill entanglement from any number of copies of $ρ$, and even with separable operations the fidelity of a two-qubit output with a Bell state never exceeds $(1+\sqrt{2})/4 \approx 0.604$. It follows that distillable entanglement is neither additive nor convex.

item.title: Neural Network Decoders For Qubit Loss
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a convolutional‑neural‑network decoder can ingest loss‑resolution data and recover the same logical error suppression as costly maximum‑likelihood methods, opening a practical path to fault‑tolerant operation on platforms where qubit loss dominates. By introducing the high‑throughput “slim” sampler, the authors extend loss‑aware decoding beyond surface codes to a 144‑qubit qLDPC bicycle code, demonstrating over three orders of magnitude improvement in logical error rates at sub‑percent physical error rates. The work bridges the gap between machine‑learning‑based decoders and realistic hardware constraints, suggesting that near‑term quantum processors could achieve much lower overheads without redesigning their error‑correction circuitry. However, the results still rely on simulated Pauli‑plus‑loss noise models, so experimental validation will be essential to confirm scalability on actual devices.

Qubit loss is a significant source of error in many quantum hardware platforms, requiring circuits that periodically replace or reset qubits to maintain fault-tolerance. When the reset process includes loss-resolving measurements, this information can improve decoding and substantially reduce overhead compared to the case where this information is not available. Prior work has demonstrated loss-tolerant circuits for the surface code that show significantly improved thresholds and subthreshold scaling by incorporating loss information. However, the computational complexity of loss simulation and decoding, which falls outside of the usual stabilizer framework, has limited extending these studies to high-rate qLDPC codes, which are already challenging to decode in the absence of loss. In this work, we present a loss-aware convolutional neural-network (CNN) decoder framework that circumvents this challenge. Training is enabled by a novel sampler, \texttt{slim}, which achieves a throughput for circuits with Pauli noise and loss that is comparable to the state-of-the-art for pure Pauli noise. On the surface code with loss, the decoder matches the accuracy of computationally expensive most-likely error (MLE) decoders at much lower latency. For the $[[144,12,12]]$ bivariate bicycle (Gross) code, we study a walking syndrome extraction circuit with Pauli and loss errors. For physical error rates $p<1\%$, we observe a more than $10^3$-fold lower logical error rate for a pure loss model, relative to a pure Pauli error model at the same physical error rate, along with significantly enhanced sub-threshold error rate scaling. This demonstrates that loss-dominated error models can also significantly improve performance in a high-rate qLDPC code, and provides a simulation and decoder training platform that can be extended to other codes and algorithmic gadgets.

item.title: The Price of Quantum Advantage in Computational Chemistry
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles the next‑stage question for quantum chemistry: not just whether a fault‑tolerant quantum computer can solve hard molecules, but when it will actually beat the cheapest classical alternatives on a realistic cost basis. By benchmarking 26 chemically relevant systems—including the notoriously difficult FeMoco cluster—against state‑of‑the‑art selected configuration interaction methods, the authors show that even at an optimistic \$7,000 per QPU‑hour most targets remain cheaper to compute classically, underscoring how crucial reliable classical baselines and careful trial‑state preparation are for any claimed quantum advantage. The work therefore provides a concrete economic yardstick that will help both researchers and policymakers gauge when quantum hardware investments become justified in computational chemistry.

As the fault-tolerant era approaches, the question shifts from ``is it possible'' to ``is it worthwhile.'' To assess practical quantum advantage against reliable classical baselines, we examine 26 benchmark instances including FeMoco, iron-sulfur clusters, cytochrome P450, and ruthenium catalysts using two selected configuration interaction solvers, SHCI and TrimCI. Comparing classical workloads with fault-tolerant resource estimates, we calculate the break-even whole-QPU hourly price. Even at an optimistic price of US\$7{,}000 per whole-QPU hour, and with mid-range CPU clusters, classical computation remains cheaper for six of seven systems. FeMoco alone remains sensitive to the classical method and extrapolation strategy. Wavefunction analysis further reveals how orbital choice affects the determinant support required for target-state overlap in quantum phase estimation (QPE). Our results highlight the importance of reliable classical references and trial-state characterization, and quantify the economic conditions under which quantum computing can become competitive with classical alternatives.

item.title: Bound magic in multi-qubit systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This paper proves that even in standard qubit hardware there exist non‑stabilizer “bound‑magic’’ states from which no pure magic can be distilled, closing a long‑standing gap that was previously only known for odd‑dimensional systems. By formulating a PPT‑like criterion that is stable under tensor products and stabilizer operations, the authors give a concrete way to identify these useless resources and explicitly construct examples for three or more qubits. The result sharpens our understanding of magic‑state distillation limits, warning designers of fault‑tolerant architectures that not all noisy non‑stabilizer states can be salvaged and motivating new protocols to avoid such bound regions.

Magic captures nonstabilizerness, a resource required for quantum computational speedups. We prove the existence of multi-qubit nonstabilizer states from which no pure magic can be distilled, even with arbitrarily many copies and rounds of stabilizer operations. Such bound magic states have previously been only known to exist in odd Hilbert-space dimensions, where positivity of discrete Wigner functions can be used analogously to the positive partial transpose (PPT) criterion for bound entanglement. We introduce a PPT analogue for magic in multi-qubit systems that is closed under tensor products and stabilizer operations and reduces to the stabilizer polytope for one and two qubits. This enables the proof of multi-qubit bound magic and the explicit construction of bound magic states for $n \geq 3$ qubits.

item.title: Localization of an Individual Charge Fluctuator in a Si/SiGe Spin Qubit Device
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first time a single charge‑noise two‑level fluctuator has been pinpointed inside a Si/SiGe spin‑qubit stack, showing that electrostatic triangulation combined with realistic simulations can locate a defect to within a few nanometres and even infer its dipole strength. By revealing that the culprit resides in the atomic‑layer‑deposited Al₂O₃ rather than the silicon channel, the work gives device engineers a concrete target for material improvements—a crucial step toward reducing charge noise and pushing gate fidelities past the fault‑tolerance threshold. The technique also opens a pathway to systematically map noisy interfaces across different qubit platforms, although its reliance on high‑resolution sensing dots may limit immediate scalability to large‑scale processors.

Charge noise from two-level fluctuators (TLFs) limits gate fidelities in semiconductor spin qubits, yet locating individual fluctuators within a device remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a spatial triangulation method that combines the gate dependence of a TLF's detuning with the chemical potential shifts it induces in a sensing dot. Applying this method to previously reported measurements from a gated Si/SiGe quantum dot device, we use electrostatic simulations to jointly constrain the fluctuator's three-dimensional position and the magnitude of its electric dipole moment. We localize the fluctuator to a region spanning 31 nm by 1 nm laterally and 4 nm vertically within the bulk of the atomic layer deposited aluminum oxide, identifying the material hosting this individual charge-noise source. The measurements are consistent with a vertically oriented TLF with a magnitude of 3 to 4 e$\mathring{A}$. This approach provides a route to determining which materials and interfaces host active charge fluctuators in semiconductor spin qubit devices.

item.title: $\mathsf{AC}^0 \not\subseteq \mathsf{BQAC}^0/\mathsf{qpoly}$ via Sublinear-Degree Pauli Approximation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article establishes the first explicit separation between constant‑depth classical circuits ( AC⁰ ) and their quantum analogue with polynomial‑size advice ( BQAC⁰/qpoly ), showing that even with arbitrary quantum help a shallow QAC⁰ circuit can do no better than inverse‑polynomial guessing on a simple monotone CNF family. The proof hinges on a new sublinear‑degree Pauli approximation technique that tightly bounds the acceptance operator of any such circuit, and it immediately yields stretched‑exponential limits on shallow quantum algorithms for distinguishing state designs or probing NLTS Hamiltonians—key benchmarks in quantum complexity and error‑correction research. By clarifying exactly how much power constant‑depth quantum circuits can (and cannot) wield, the work sharpens our understanding of the frontier between feasible near‑term hardware and provably hard computational tasks.

We prove $\mathsf{AC}^0 \not\subseteq \mathsf{BQAC}^0/\mathsf{qpoly}$ in the single-copy, single-output model via an explicit $\mathsf{P}$-uniform family of linear-size monotone depth-2 CNFs. Every $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuit with arbitrary quantum advice achieves only an inverse-polynomial worst-case advantage over random guessing on this family. To prove this, we approximate the acceptance operator of any such circuit in operator norm by an advice-independent Hermitian operator of sublinear Pauli degree on a designated register alone, with degree exponent independent of width. Product-projection localization and Pauli twirling produce an auxiliary-register spectral cutoff that folds into contractions during backward peeling. The same approximation yields two stretched-exponential bounds against $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits on $m$-qubit states. First, given polynomially many copies and input-independent quantum advice, single-output circuits distinguish exact or exponentially approximate state $2$-designs from Haar-random states with advantage at most $e^{-m^α}$. Second, any state prepared from fewer than $k$ arbitrary input qubits and remaining $|0\rangle$ inputs has spectral weight at most $2e^{-m^α}$ in a constant-energy-density band of an Anshu--Breuckmann--Nirkhe NLTS Hamiltonian encoding $k$ logical qubits. Both bounds hold for every fixed $α\in(0,1)$.

item.title: Fewer Parameters, Longer Runtimes: The Wall-Clock Cost of Hybrid Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Networks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article cuts through the hype around hybrid quantum‑classical physics‑informed neural networks by showing that fewer trainable parameters do not translate into faster training when the quantum circuit is simulated on classical hardware. By benchmarking forward passes and gradient calculations on a diffusion problem, the authors demonstrate that even modestly sized hybrids can be an order of magnitude slower than both pure classical PINNs and size‑matched classical controls—a stark reminder that wall‑clock time, not parameter count, will determine near‑term usefulness. The results underscore the urgent need for more efficient quantum simulators or real quantum processors before hybrid QML approaches can claim a practical advantage in scientific computing workloads.

While hybrid quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks (QCPINNs) are often described as efficient because they have fewer trainable parameters than classical PINNs, parameter count does not measure wall-clock cost. To examine this gap on a one-dimensional seawater temperature diffusion benchmark, with the quantum circuits simulated on a CPU, we time the four cumulative stages a PINN needs (the forward pass, the first- and second-order input gradients, and the PDE-loss parameter gradient) for a classical PINN, four hybrid configurations that differ in qubit count and circuit depth, and size-matched classical controls that share the hybrids' classical layers. We find that the hybrids are 14-56x slower than the classical PINN for the forward pass and 10-97x slower for the PDE-loss parameter gradient, and even against the size-matched controls, they remain 9-85x slower. Further, over the tested ranges, runtime increased approximately exponentially with qubit count, approximately linearly with circuit depth, and sub-linearly with batch size, while for the circuit-only forward pass, a second simulator backend was 10-165x slower under the same calling pattern. Although the hybrids have 38-44% fewer parameters than the classical PINN, this reduction comes from their smaller classical layers, as the quantum circuit accounts for at most 2.5% of each hybrid's parameters. Yet parameter count failed to predict runtime even among the classical networks, since the size-matched controls, despite having fewer parameters than the classical PINN, run slower than it. Our conclusion is that fewer parameters did not mean lower cost: every hybrid took at least ten times longer than the classical PINN at every stage, and the gap grew quickly with the number of qubits.

item.title: Experimental Quantum Hardware Benchmarks of Flat Non-Clifford Hypergraph States, Antipodal Obstructions, and Nonlocal Games on IBM Heron r2
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reports the first large‑scale hardware benchmarks of genuinely non‑Clifford hypergraph states on IBM’s 156‑qubit Heron r2 processors, demonstrating contextuality and coherence far beyond random baselines for up to 16 entangled qubits. By extending the Clifford‑only demonstrations such as Google’s magic‑square experiment, it provides a concrete proof‑of‑principle that near‑term devices can generate and verify the algebraic invariants needed for fault‑tolerant algorithms that rely on non‑Clifford resources. The results also highlight how calibration‑aware layout and barrier‑protected Loschmidt echoes can push win rates close to 97 %, though they still lag behind Willow’s record, underscoring both progress and the remaining scaling challenges.

Real-hardware demonstrations of quantum contextuality have reached high precision on superconducting processors, exemplified by Google Quantum AI's Mermin-Peres magic square and stabilizer games on Willow (Science, 2026). Extending such benchmarks beyond the Clifford regime requires non-Clifford hypergraph states |ψ_f> = 2^{-n/2} \sum_x (-1)^{f(x)} |x> governed by discrete algebraic invariants. Building on our Lean 4-verified framework of Modular Walsh Rigidity and Antipodal Obstructions, we present an experimental study on two 156-qubit IBM Heron r2 processors (ibm_fez, ibm_kingston) across 3 to 50 qubits and 11 auditable jobs (2.13 RUs total). First, we verify antipodal obstructions and mod-17 Walsh rigidity for degree-3/4 states (n=6,8,10), observing 5.4x-11.6x X-basis flatness separation between bent states, obstructed controls, and a degree-4 mod-3 fooler (W = +-1 mod 3), plus n=7 nonlinearity extraction (54.83 vs. 56.00). Second, barrier-protected Loschmidt echoes confirm non-Clifford coherence up to genuinely entangled 16-qubit degree-4 states (1,488x above random on ibm_fez; 17,296x on ibm_kingston for 2x8q, a 2.87x cross-chip gain) and locate a Heavy-Hex depth-513 coherence cliff. Third, calibration-aware layout raises the raw Mermin-Peres win rate on ibm_fez to 96.85 +- 0.09% raw (+87.4 sigma above 88.89% classical; 1.45 pp below Willow's 98.30% raw), while a tensored SPAM diagnostic reaches 98.35%. Uniformly random even-weight GHZ parity games beat the classical bound up to n=30 (89.44% [+79.4 sigma] at 6q to 59.46 +- 0.54% [+17.4 sigma] at 30q). item.title: LatentRL-QAS: Transfer via Latent Reinforcement Learning for Quantum Architecture Search
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that quantum circuit design can finally scale across qubit counts by moving the reinforcement‑learning search into a size‑invariant latent space, eliminating the combinatorial blow‑up that has hampered previous QAS methods. By encoding any‑size circuits with a variational autoencoder and refreshing the latent representation as new solutions emerge, LatentRL‑QAS transfers knowledge from small to larger systems and discovers five‑ and six‑qubit absolutely maximally entangled states far more efficiently than even vastly larger baseline agents. The breakthrough points toward practical, automated synthesis of error‑correcting resources on near‑term devices, though its performance under realistic noise models beyond depolarisation remains to be validated.

Reinforcement learning (RL) emerges as a prominent approach to quantum architecture search (QAS), the automated design of quantum circuits. However, transferring what an agent has learned from one number of qubits to another is still weakly explored: the state, the action space and the neural network of a state-of-the-art RL-QAS agent all grow with the number of qubits, which makes transfer learning across qubit counts prohibitive. We make this transfer possible by introducing LatentRL-QAS, a latent space transfer and refresh framework for RL-based QAS. At its core, a circuit variational autoencoder encodes a circuit as one token per gate and maps circuits on any number of qubits into the same latent space. An RL agent navigates this space instead of adding gates, so its state, actions and network have the same size at every qubit count. The latent space is periodically refreshed with the agent's new discoveries and, for a larger system, grown from the solutions of the smaller one, so what is transferred is the representation of circuits, not network weights or past experience. To show transfer, we consider absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states, a resource for quantum error correction. LatentRL-QAS discovers the five- and six-qubit AME states without being shown them and prepares them in 89-99% of evaluation episodes, whereas the baseline RL-QAS fails to find them with the same budget, even with a network 10 to 17 times larger. LatentRL-QAS remains robust under depolarizing noise with single-qubit gate errors amplified 10x and two-qubit gate errors 5x compared with IBM quantum hardware. By decoupling the RL agent from the number of qubits, LatentRL-QAS lets quantum architecture search reuse circuit representations learned on smaller problems, providing a foundation for the transferable design of circuits across quantum optimization problems.

item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that bivariate bicycle codes—already known for their lower qubit overhead compared to surface codes—can be decoded at microsecond‑scale speeds even under realistic circuit‑level noise, thanks to a highly optimized parallel‑window GPU engine. By achieving a 120× boost over traditional sliding‑window decoders and reducing logical failure rates by up to 36% relative to prior belief‑propagation methods, the work narrows the gap between theoretical error‑correction thresholds and the real‑time processing required for scalable quantum processors. The results suggest that commodity GPUs could become a practical backend for on‑the‑fly decoding in near‑term devices, although performance will still depend on hardware generation and the ability to map larger code families onto similar architectures.

Bivariate bicycle (BB) codes reduce the physical-qubit overhead of quantum error correction compared to other codes such as Surface codes, but circuit-level faults create dependencies across measurement rounds that limit decoding throughput. We present a parallel-window GPU decoder that combines reusable fault patterns, compact shared-memory state, and persistent GPU workers using min-sum with Relay-BP recovery. On an RTX 5090, the proposed decoder keeps pace with one syndrome round every 1 $μ$s across all four evaluated codes, up to [[144,12,12]] with 63-144 $μ$s median commit delays. This rate has not been demonstrated in prior circuit-level GPU decoding studies and it provides $120\times$ higher decoding throughput than sequential sliding-window decoding. Checking neighboring detector rounds before accepting a decoding result reduces failure rates by up to 65%. For [[144,12,12]] at $p=0.002$, our proposed decoder achieves $7.58\times 10^{-6}$ failures per round, 36% lower than the published belief propagation (BP) with syndrome flipping (BP-SF) result.

item.title: Native higher-order optimization with entropy quantum computing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that entropy‑based quantum computing can natively encode cubic and quartic objective functions—something that forces annealers into costly quadratization and gate‑model processors into deep circuit compilations. By solving six industrial‑scale instances on the Dirac‑3S photonic‑electronic platform, including a portfolio problem with 80 000 terms, the authors demonstrate feasible solutions within 0.32 % of the best known values while avoiding embeddings that would demand >10⁵ physical qubits or millions of two‑qubit gates on other hardware. The result opens a practical pathway for tackling higher‑order optimization problems on near‑term quantum devices, though further work is needed to assess scalability and error robustness as problem sizes grow.

Higher-order interactions are common in applied optimization: parity checks, radar-code sidelobes, portfolio skewness and kurtosis, and marketing-channel synergies all yield cubic or quartic objectives. Quantum annealers and most Ising machines accept only quadratic objectives, and gate-based quantum processors build every higher-order term from two-qubit gates. Entropy quantum computing, realized in the hybrid photonic-electronic Dirac-3S system, accepts polynomials of degree up to five with all-to-all coupling over binary, integer or simplex-constrained continuous variables. No user-supplied quadratization or circuit compilation is needed. We formulate four industrial use cases as six cubic and quartic instances, run them on Dirac-3S with 30 samples each, and score every sample against a certified optimum or a classical best-known value. We also estimate their cost on quantum annealers, superconducting grids and trapped-ion registers under standard mappings. For the two densest instances, a portfolio with about 80,000 terms and a budget allocation with 360,000 terms, the quadratized problems need embeddings far beyond current annealers, over $10^5$ physical qubits for the portfolio alone, and one phase-separation layer costs over $10^6$ two-qubit gates before optimization. Dirac-3S ran all six natively and returned feasible, distinct solutions. All samples of the binary instances are single-flip local minima. The best portfolio sample lies within 0.32% of the best-known value and the best budget sample 15% above it, but no sample reached its reference. Classical solvers reach the references within minutes at these sizes, and random starts followed by a local polish reach comparable or better values, so the advantage established here is one of expressibility and mapping cost, not of solution quality. Whether it extends to time to solution at larger sizes remains open.

item.title: Intrinsically nonlinear nanomechanical resonator toward the single-phonon Kerr regime
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that nanomechanical resonators can exhibit a sizable intrinsic Kerr nonlinearity, eliminating the need for externally engineered anharmonicity that typically introduces extra loss and decoherence. By quantifying the onset of mechanical bistability at just a few dozen phonons and showing how to tune it via the nanotube’s polarization angle, the work pushes the field toward the long‑sought single‑phonon Kerr regime where purely mechanical Schrödinger‑cat states and coherent qubits become feasible. If the extrapolation to shorter resonators holds up experimentally, it could provide a low‑noise, scalable hardware platform that complements superconducting and photonic quantum processors.

Manipulating a physical system at the single-quantum level typically requires an anharmonic energy spectrum. Nanomechanical resonators, however, are commonly admitted to be linear objects in the single-phonon regime, thus motivating most efforts to employ external sources of nonlinearity at the cost of added relaxation and decoherence channels. Here, we take a radically different approach by directly exploiting strong intrinsic mechanical nonlinearities. We quantify this nonlinearity using a novel method based on the coupling between bending modes. Using this technique, we establish an upper bound of 34.0 +/- 9.7 phonons for the onset of intrinsically mechanical bistability. In addition, we highlight a new tuning mechanism based on a mechanical polarization angle of an upward-buckled nanotube resonator allowing us to reach an optimal working point. Extrapolating this level of intrinsic nonlinearity to realistically shorter resonators shows that the single-phonon Kerr regime is within reach, allowing for the realization of purely mechanical Schrödinger-cat states and highly coherent mechanical qubits.

item.title: Quantum Algorithm for Direct Estimation of Energy-Level Differences via Quantum Dynamics Simulation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a fault‑tolerant‑ready algorithm that extracts tiny energy gaps—such as molecular force constants—directly from a pair of time‑evolution circuits, cutting the sampling cost from the full Hamiltonian norm to the much smaller norm of its derivative. By sidestepping the heavy overhead of statistical phase estimation for differences, it promises faster, lower‑qubit calculations of gradients that are essential for geometry optimisation and materials design, complementing recent advances in quantum gradient‐estimation and variational chemistry methods. The numerical results on the Fermi‑Hubbard model suggest a practical pathway to obtain accurate forces on early quantum hardware, though scaling to larger, chemically realistic systems will still depend on improvements in error rates and Hamiltonian simulation techniques.

We present a quantum algorithm for the early fault-tolerant quantum computing (early-FTQC) era that estimates minute energy-level differences, such as energy gradients and molecular forces, at a lower sampling cost than existing phase-estimation methods. Such energy derivatives, accessed as the small energy difference induced by an infinitesimal parameter shift, are central to quantum simulation in chemistry and materials science. Although Statistical Phase Estimation (SPE) is well-suited to energy estimation in this era, applying it to an energy difference demands a sampling complexity that scales with the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian, which grows with system size. Our algorithm overcomes this by incorporating two time-evolution operators, corresponding to the Hamiltonians before and after the parameter shift, into a single quantum circuit, which is combined with a non-adaptive, statistically sampled reconstruction in the energy-difference domain. This reduces the relevant scale from the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian to that of the operator norm of the Hamiltonian derivative and the parameter shift, thereby lowering the sampling complexity. We further propose the joint estimation of energy eigenvalues and their differences, giving a holistic view of the energy landscape. Numerical simulations and resource estimations on prototypical systems, such as the Fermi-Hubbard model, demonstrate the resulting reductions in required resources without compromising precision. This positions energy-difference estimation as a practical task for early-FTQC devices, opening a route to molecular forces, response properties, and excited-state energy differences.

item.title: Geometry, masking and selection in Differential Evolution and SOMA on quantum state manifolds
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that tailoring classic evolutionary heuristics to the true geometry of quantum‑state spaces can turn modest optimisers into high‑performing workhorses, with full‑crossover DE jumping from sub‑50 % success on periodic problems to a perfect record and boosting variational eigensolver accuracy by 90 % for only a few percent extra runtime. By replacing Euclidean subtraction with manifold‑aware angular or geodesic differences, the authors demonstrate a concrete pathway to more reliable hybrid quantum–classical optimisation—a hot topic as VQE and QAOA scale up. The results suggest that geometry‑consistent operators may become a standard upgrade for evolutionary algorithms, though their overhead and scalability beyond six qubits still need systematic testing.

Differential Evolution (DE) and the Self-Organizing Migrating Algorithm (SOMA) generate new candidates through vector arithmetic: they subtract population members, scale the difference, and mask coordinates. Many practical search spaces are not vector spaces, however. Rotation angles are periodic, normalized states lie on spheres and projective spaces, and circuit parameters are coupled through the quantum states they produce. We present a systematic study of how such geometry affects the core operations of DE and SOMA. Keeping the operators and selection rules fixed, we replace only their geometric primitives and separate the effects of difference construction, masking, and selection in a large paired numerical study covering textbook manifolds and variational quantum problems. Geometry-consistent differences make full-crossover (CR = 1) DE significantly better on 16 of 31 non-Euclidean configurations, with no significant deterioration, and the advantage persists when the measured computational cost of each variant is taken into account. The effect is largest where ordinary subtraction misrepresents distances between candidates: success on periodic synchronization rises from 44% to 100%, and on a positive-definite matrix problem from 1% to 99%. On six- qubit variational eigensolvers, shortest-path angular differences reduce the mean final loss by 90% for about 3% extra runtime. The improvements come with two contrasting diversity patterns, more effective population contraction or preserved population diversity, so higher acceptance rates do not necessarily indicate better search. Crossover masks interact with geometry: they can favor cheaper retractions and can increase the distance moved in quantum-state space when circuit parameters are coupled. These results give practical rules for designing population-based optimizers on non-Euclidean and quantum search spaces.

item.title: Quantum-centric assessment of saturated ferromagnetism beyond the flat-band limit
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that near‑term quantum processors can tackle genuinely hard many‑body problems by mapping a 64‑qubit sawtooth Hubbard chain onto a configuration‑interaction subspace that is orders of magnitude smaller than the full Hilbert space yet still captures saturated ferromagnetism with >97 % fidelity. By quantifying how the critical on‑site repulsion scales with band dispersion (U≈2W) and establishing a rigorous lower bound for a 4×3 decorated lattice, the work bridges a gap between ideal flat‑band theory and realistic materials where bandwidth cannot be ignored. The results showcase both a concrete benchmark for quantum hardware and a pathway toward using quantum simulations to predict magnetic phases in correlated electron systems.

Saturated ferromagnetism has been proven for every on-site repulsion $U > 0$ in Hubbard models with a flat lowest band, and the interaction required for it grows with the band width $W$ when the band becomes dispersive. We study the dispersive case at quarter filling by quantum-selected configuration interaction and sample-based quantum diagonalization with IBM Quantum's Heron processors, focusing on the quantized square of the total spin of the computed states. We treat a sawtooth chain of 16 unit cells on 64 qubits, whose full configuration space of $1.1\times 10^{14}$ determinants exceeds that of one of the largest full configuration interaction calculations, and obtain the stability diagram of saturated ferromagnetism on the decorated square lattice in the plane of $U$ and $W$. For the chain, a subspace of only $3\times 10^{-5}$ of the full configuration space gives a state with more than $97\%$ of its weight in the sector of maximal spin. For the decorated square lattice of $4\times 3$ unit cells on 48 qubits, the computed states in subspaces of less than $1\%$ of the full configuration space switch from low-spin states to nearly fully polarized states at $U \simeq 2W$. The calculations also give a rigorous lower bound of $1.9W$ on the critical interaction of the $4\times 3$ lattice.

item.title: Prospects and limitations of adaptive variational quantum algorithms for lattice field theories: a case study in 2+1 dimensions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the popular ADAPT‑VQE approach, which has already enabled proof‑of‑principle vacuum preparation in one‑dimensional gauge models, runs into two fundamental roadblocks when pushed to realistic 2+1‑D lattice field theories: real‑valued operator pools become blind to gradient information and the algorithm can mistakenly lock onto excited states. By diagnosing these issues with concrete examples—including free Wilson fermions—and demonstrating that adding charge‑conjugation symmetry to the pool (or mixing pools with tailored initial states) restores reliable ground‑state convergence, the work provides the first practical recipe for scaling variational quantum simulations beyond 1+1 dimensions. These insights are crucial for anyone aiming to use near‑term quantum hardware to tackle higher‑dimensional lattice gauge problems, as they clarify both the limits of current methods and concrete steps to overcome them.

The variational quantum algorithm ADAPT-VQE has previously been used to prepare the vacuum of lattice gauge theories in $1+1D$. In this paper, we study whether it extends to higher dimensions. We identify two general limitations of ADAPT-VQE. First, if the qubit Hamiltonian and the initial state are real, i.e., invariant under qubit-level time-reversal, all real-valued pool operators have vanishing gradients and are never selected. Second, the algorithm can converge to excited eigenstates. We illustrate both limitations, also providing examples from literature, and present a first application of ADAPT-VQE to a lattice field theory in $2+1D$, namely free Wilson fermions, where both obstacles occur. Adding charge conjugation symmetry to the operator pool improves the results, and combining different pools with suitable initial states recovers the ground and first excited states over the full mass range. These findings give practical guidelines for applying ADAPT-VQE to lattice field theories beyond $1+1D$.

item.title: A Koashi--Imoto Criterion for Holevo-Rate Visible Compression
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a long‑standing question in quantum source coding by giving an exact, operational condition—via the Koashi–Imoto decomposition—for when the optimal Holevo rate can be reached without entanglement assistance, simply using shared randomness. The result clarifies that for qubit ensembles the only way to hit the Holevo limit is if the signals are all pure or mutually commuting, a restriction that directly informs the design of hardware‑efficient compression protocols and error‑tolerant quantum networking stacks. By linking visible compression to recent recovery and decoupling techniques, it also bridges foundational information theory with practical coding strategies, though the bound shows that any mixed component forces a non‑negligible rate penalty regardless of block length.

For a finite memoryless quantum source whose encoder knows the sequence of classical labels, we determine when the Holevo rate is achievable with shared classical randomness and no shared entanglement. In the maximal Koashi--Imoto decomposition of the signal ensemble, this occurs exactly when each signal is pure on the quantum part of every sector it occupies. For qubits, this means that the signals are all pure or commute pairwise. If any occupied quantum part is mixed, every code with sufficiently small mean local error has rate bounded away from the Holevo information, uniformly in blocklength. To prove the converse, we apply Fawzi--Renner recovery to a hypothetical sequence of visible codes approaching the Holevo rate at vanishing local error, then invoke a decoupling bound of Baghali Khanian and Winter for blind compression.

item.title: Classical algorithms for sparse random Hamiltonians via free probability
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that for a broad class of sparse random Hamiltonians—a setting long thought to demand quantum simulation—classical algorithms can match quantum runtimes up to sub‑exponential precision, narrowing the gap between classical and quantum performance on average‑case many‑body problems. By leveraging free probability to extract long‑time dynamics from short‑time data, the authors sidestep the usual exponential blow‑up associated with sign problems, entanglement growth, or low‑temperature regimes that cripple tensor‑network methods. The result sharpens our understanding of where genuine quantum advantage may lie and suggests new classical tools for benchmarking quantum hardware, though it remains limited to random, non‑local models rather than structured Hamiltonians encountered in chemistry or materials science.

The search for quantum advantage in average-case problems is a pressing open question in physics and computer science. The widest conjectured example of such an advantage is in simulation of quantum many-body systems, where sign problems and entanglement growth cause the breakdown of many classical methods. Nonetheless, theoretical evidence for or against such an advantage remains scarce. Here, we investigate this in sparse random non-local Hamiltonians. We design a classical algorithm for such Hamiltonians that enables accurate computation of spectral fluctuations, thermal values, and time-ordered and out-of-time-order correlation functions. For any subexponential precision $\varepsilon$, our algorithm runs in time $(1/\varepsilon)^{2+o(1)}$, nearly identical to a quantum simulation. Crucially, this applies even at late evolution times, low temperatures, and near critical points, where existing classical methods require exponential time. Rather than directly simulating a quantum state or operator, our algorithm first computes the model's mean behavior and then a short hierarchy of instance-dependent corrections. These corrections predict long-time behavior based on short-time data using free probability theory.

item.title: Class-resolved sifting for quantum key distribution with photon pairs hyperentangled in polarization and transverse spatial variables
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how class‑resolved sifting can unlock the full two‑bit per‑pair capacity of photon pairs hyperentangled in polarization and transverse spatial modes, turning what was previously treated as separate “high‑dimensional” channels into a single, efficiently usable key source. By analysing each degree of freedom independently yet simultaneously, the authors expose subtle basis‑dependent side‑channels that arise from the measurement apparatus—a diagnostic that is increasingly important as QKD moves toward multi‑degree‑of‑freedom implementations and higher data rates. The technique dovetails with recent advances in orbital‑angular‑momentum and other high‑dimensional QKD schemes, offering a practical pathway to boost key yields while maintaining rigorous security bounds, though its statistical sensitivity still limits detection of very weak cross‑couplings.

Photon pairs hyperentangled in polarization and transverse spatial variables can carry two key bits per pair in entanglement-based quantum key distribution. We develop class-resolved sifting for such sources: every detected pair is assigned to a class according to which degrees of freedom were measured in compatible bases, and error and key rates are estimated separately in each class. Applied to previously reported data from a two-crystal spontaneous parametric down-conversion source read out in intermediate fractional-Fourier planes, the method recovers the key yield of independent sifting and turns the comparison between classes into a quantitative consistency test for cross-dependencies between the two degrees of freedom. The measured dependence lies below the spatial-polarization coupling predicted for the source, at the edge of the present statistical sensitivity. Resolving the data by polarization-analyzer setting, we find an approximately twofold dependence of the spatial error on the polarization setting in one readout arm, attributable to the measurement apparatus rather than to the source and relevant to basis-dependent side channels. We compare the hyperentangled protocol with a single 4-dimensional system measured in two mutually unbiased bases. Fundamentally, both yield the same key per detected pair and obey the same entropic bound, but they differ in their tensor-product structure: hyperentanglement factors the bases into separate two-outcome measurements, which are simpler to implement and allow errors to be attributed to each degree of freedom, whereas a single variable gives access to non-product bases that can increase the noise tolerance. For the present source, whose polarization coherence is limited by partial which-crystal erasure, a single-variable spatial encoding would yield more key only if its four-outcome readout kept the symbol error within a few percent.

item.title: Trotterized hybrid qubit-boson simulation of the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard model
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a practical route to simulate light‑matter lattice models on near‑term quantum hardware by combining qubit and bosonic registers in a Trotterized circuit, something that has only recently become feasible with tools like Bosonic Qiskit and matrix‑product‑state backends. By benchmarking single‑polariton transport, two‑excitation dynamics under hard‑core constraints, and entanglement growth against exact diagonalization, the authors show that hybrid qubit‑boson simulations can capture nontrivial many‑body physics while remaining tractable on classical simulators. The work therefore paves the way for experimentalists to explore more complex, possibly open, photonic quantum systems on emerging platforms that natively support both qubits and bosonic modes.

The Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard (JCH) model describes the interaction of light and matter in coupled optical cavities and provides a framework for studying their quantum dynamics. In this work, we design a Trotterized quantum circuit to investigate the real-time dynamics of the JCH model using Bosonic Qiskit and a Matrix Product State (MPS) backend. We simulate single-polariton transport and benchmark site occupations against exact diagonalization results. We then extend the simulations to the two-excitation sector under a hard-core photon constraint, examining excitation transport and symmetry properties. Finally, we study the dependence of bipartite entanglement entropy on the inter-cavity photon-hopping strength. The results illustrate how hybrid qubit-boson circuits, simulated with matrix product states, can be used to study light-matter lattice dynamics. This work provides a numerical benchmark for extending hybrid simulation approaches to more complex interacting and open light-matter systems.

item.title: Perturbative unitarity bounds from qubit entanglement in scalar scattering and QED
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that the entanglement generated between qubit‑encoded particle spins in simple scalar and QED scattering can be used as a quantitative probe of perturbative unitarity, yielding coupling‑constant limits that are often tighter than traditional partial‑wave bounds. By tracing out momentum and analysing the resulting quantum channel, the authors turn a textbook scattering problem into a concrete testbed for quantum information techniques, suggesting new ways to benchmark and validate quantum simulators that aim to emulate relativistic field theories. The approach also sidesteps the notorious forward‑scattering singularities that plague conventional analyses, offering a cleaner theoretical handle that could inform both high‑energy phenomenology and the design of hardware‑efficient algorithms for scattering simulations.

In the framework of $2\to 2$ relativistic scattering described by the perturbative $S$-matrix, we perform a comprehensive analysis of the properties of quantum channels obtained by tracing out the momentum from the scattered state. We work in two distinct scenarios with qubit degrees of freedom: flavored scalar contact interactions and QED, focusing in particular on initial-state leptons with transverse polarization. We identify the conditions that make the quantum channel unitary, calculate the entanglement of the qubits through the concurrence, and use its maximally allowed value to extract perturbativity upper bounds on the coupling constants. We find that the limits are often more constraining than the corresponding partial-wave expansion bounds, and that they allow us to bypass some of the obstacles associated in the latter with the singular behavior of forward scattering.

item.title: Programmable multipartite entanglement analogues
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a reconfigurable metasurface that can program the number and type of coherently linked degrees of freedom in a classical electromagnetic field, achieving Bell‑like and GHZ‑like states up to five parties—the highest multipartite order yet realized in optics without genuine quantum entanglement. By making multipartiteness itself tunable across polarization, frequency, orbital angular momentum, wavevector direction and envelope modes, the work provides a versatile testbed for probing the structure of complex quantum correlations using lossless, room‑temperature light. It bridges recent advances in programmable photonic metasurfaces with the need for scalable platforms to benchmark multipartite protocols, offering a low‑cost sandbox for algorithm development while reminding readers that the underlying physics remains classical rather than nonlocal.

Quantum entanglement underpins the quantum information science. Its multipartite forms distribute coherence across several subsystems, but controlling their composition and order is increasingly difficult as more subsystems participate. Classical nonseparable waves provide accessible analogues of these structures, although existing implementations largely fix the participating degrees of freedom through their generating architectures. Here we overcome this constraint by making multipartiteness itself programmable in electromagnetic fields. A spatiotemporal metasurface reconfigures the identity and number of coherently linked state spaces independently across polarization, frequency, orbital angular momentum, wavevector direction, and orthogonal envelope modes. We realize complete Bell-like and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger-like families from bipartite to five-partite order and exchange constituents at fixed order. To our knowledge, the five-partite state has the highest multipartite order experimentally realized in classical electromagnetic fields. These results establish the distribution of coherence across physical state spaces as a programmable property of classical waves and provide a platform for studying selected structures of multipartite quantum states without invoking quantum entanglement or nonlocality.

item.title: Classical sampling of verifiable graph-state quantum advantage experiments
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the current “verifiable quantum‑advantage” proposals can still be outpaced by modest classical hardware, underscoring how delicate the balance between verifiability and hardness truly is. By exploiting the built‑in error‑detection structure, the authors classically sampled the 70‑qubit graph‑state experiment with higher fidelity than IBM’s own processor, revealing that T‑gate placement—forced to hide from the verifier—leaves a tractable tail for classical simulators. The work therefore maps a concrete obstacle for future advantage demonstrations and signals that any next‑generation verifiable benchmark must deliberately scramble or conceal non‑Clifford resources to avoid such classical shortcuts.

Quantum computers are expected to outperform classical ones on some tasks, but a convincing demonstration must be both hard to reproduce classically and verifiable. A recent proposal achieves verifiability by preparing graph states with built-in error detection, so that the quality of the experiment can be certified without simulating it; hardness is added by measuring in a non-Clifford basis or by inserting T gates. We show that the two instances posted to demonstrate this proposal on IBM hardware can be sampled classically on eight graphics processing units, with higher quality than the hardware in comparable or shorter time. For the 70-qubit instance our samples are drawn from the ideal output distribution; for the 64-qubit instance with 314 T gates they come with a certified fidelity of at least 0.908, against 0.349 for the hardware. The reason lies in verification itself: T gates can only be placed where the error detection cannot see them, which pushes them towards the end of the circuit, where they add little classical cost. Our results identify the features that future verifiable advantage experiments must control.
